00:14:45.270 --> 00:14:49.230
by sending an email and copying in the entire company.

277
00:14:49.230 --> 00:14:51.930
This sent a huge amount of negative energy

278
00:14:51.930 --> 00:14:55.317
and I think it showed a lack of emotional intelligence."

279
00:14:57.150 --> 00:15:00.150
I wonder what you think about that scenario.

280
00:15:00.150 --> 00:15:02.913
How could the manager have dealt with this better?

281
00:15:09.990 --> 00:15:12.140
I mean, that was a pretty terrible situation, wasn't it?

282
00:15:12.140 --> 00:15:14.070
It must have been really humiliating

283
00:15:14.070 --> 00:15:17.430
and scary for him to have that mistake shown

284
00:15:17.430 --> 00:15:19.260
to the whole company.

285
00:15:19.260 --> 00:15:22.080
Perhaps the manager with a bit more emotional intelligence

286
00:15:22.080 --> 00:15:24.780
could have paused, thought about that

287
00:15:24.780 --> 00:15:26.130
and talked to him directly

288
00:15:26.130 --> 00:15:27.900
and helped him understand the mistake

289
00:15:27.900 --> 00:15:30.753
rather than humiliate him in front of everybody.

290
00:15:33.570 --> 00:15:35.220
True or false?

291
00:15:35.220 --> 00:15:38.700
Emotional intelligence is the inability to understand

292
00:15:38.700 --> 00:15:40.923
and manage emotions effectively.

293
00:15:45.870 --> 00:15:47.490
Excellent, that's false, isn't it?

294
00:15:47.490 --> 00:15:50.940
Because actually emotional intelligence is the ability

295
00:15:50.940 --> 00:15:54.210
to understand and manage emotions effectively.

296
00:15:54.210 --> 00:15:56.283
Brilliant if you got that right.

297
00:15:58.950 --> 00:16:02.310
Laura and Jacob continue the interview with Hanuman Dass.

298
00:16:02.310 --> 00:16:04.800
They say, "How do you apply your values

299
00:16:04.800 --> 00:16:07.947
through your work in finance and also Go Dharmic?"

300
00:16:09.150 --> 00:16:12.600
He says, "Dharma is at the heart of everything.

301
00:16:12.600 --> 00:16:15.480
This ancient Indian concept helps us understand

302
00:16:15.480 --> 00:16:17.580
we are all connected.

303
00:16:17.580 --> 00:16:20.040
The dharma of humanity is our purpose,

304
00:16:20.040 --> 00:16:22.173
and that purpose is to be humane.

305
00:16:23.130 --> 00:16:26.880
Dharmic values of honesty, nonviolence, or ahimsa,

306
00:16:26.880 --> 00:16:29.490
and self-control help me show integrity

307
00:16:29.490 --> 00:16:31.107
through all my work."

308
00:16:32.850 --> 00:16:36.120
So this idea of dharma is central to Hanuman Dass,

309
00:16:36.120 --> 00:16:39.810
the idea that our human purpose is to be humane

310
00:16:39.810 --> 00:16:42.360
and that if we can live with values such as honesty

311
00:16:42.360 --> 00:16:43.590
and non-violence,

312
00:16:43.590 --> 00:16:46.290
we'll actually be able to work in everything we do.

313
00:16:46.290 --> 00:16:48.840
And for Hanuman Dass, that's in his work in finance

314
00:16:48.840 --> 00:16:50.763
and his charitable work as well.

315
00:16:53.160 --> 00:16:56.490
Hanuman explains how he applies these dharmic values

316
00:16:56.490 --> 00:16:57.603
in finance.

317
00:16:58.680 --> 00:17:01.290
He says, "In finance there are high levels

318
00:17:01.290 --> 00:17:02.850
of responsibility.

319
00:17:02.850 --> 00:17:06.213
There can be opportunities to be greedy or dishonest.

320
00:17:07.110 --> 00:17:10.290
In Hindu philosophy, prosperity or artha

321
00:17:10.290 --> 00:17:12.660
is one of the goals of life.

322
00:17:12.660 --> 00:17:15.240
Artha is essential for supporting family

323
00:17:15.240 --> 00:17:17.550
and contributing to society.

324
00:17:17.550 --> 00:17:20.160
To gain wealth is a blessing,

325
00:17:20.160 --> 00:17:23.640
however, artha must be in line with dharma.

326
00:17:23.640 --> 00:17:26.370
This means wealth should be earned honestly

327
00:17:26.370 --> 00:17:30.417
and used to help others rather than just selfishly."

328
00:17:33.030 --> 00:17:36.510
So what does Hanuman Dass say here about wealth

329
00:17:36.510 --> 00:17:37.983
in Hindu philosophy?

330
00:17:39.660 --> 00:17:42.270
You might want to read this again slowly and carefully

331
00:17:42.270 --> 00:17:45.390
and see what he's saying it says philosophically

332
00:17:45.390 --> 00:17:47.763
and what that means for him practically.

333
00:17:53.790 --> 00:17:57.720
So he's saying that to become prosperous is not problematic.

334
00:17:57.720 --> 00:18:00.240
In Hindu philosophy, it's one of the goals of life

335
00:18:00.240 --> 00:18:02.940
because becoming wealthy, becoming prosperous,

336
00:18:02.940 --> 00:18:05.190
allows you to support people and contribute

337
00:18:05.190 --> 00:18:07.020
and it's seen as a blessing.

338
00:18:07.020 --> 00:18:11.100
But that wealth must be done in line with dharmic values,

339
00:18:11.100 --> 00:18:13.230
which means being earned honestly,

340
00:18:13.230 --> 00:18:15.240
not through greed or dishonesty,

341
00:18:15.240 --> 00:18:17.070
and as well as supporting your family,

342
00:18:17.070 --> 00:18:18.660
being used to help others,

343
00:18:18.660 --> 00:18:21.903
rather than just keeping all that money yourself selfishly.

344
00:18:24.870 --> 00:18:28.170
Laura and Jacob ask Hanuman, "How do dharma

345
00:18:28.170 --> 00:18:29.787
and finance connect?"

346
00:18:30.630 --> 00:18:32.790
Hanuman says, "When investing,

347
00:18:32.790 --> 00:18:35.640
I apply the dharmic value of ahimsa.

348
00:18:35.640 --> 00:18:38.130
I consider if the company supports the arms trade

349
00:18:38.130 --> 00:18:40.020
or the animal industry.

350
00:18:40.020 --> 00:18:43.050
Just considering a monetary gain is shortsighted,

351
00:18:43.050 --> 00:18:45.870
I need to look at ways of not causing harm.

352
00:18:45.870 --> 00:18:48.240
I'd be looking to invest in energy efficient companies

353
00:18:48.240 --> 00:18:50.280
such as wind or solar.

354
00:18:50.280 --> 00:18:52.860
It's important for me to speak honestly with companies

355
00:18:52.860 --> 00:18:56.877
to help them transition rather than simply criticize."

356
00:18:58.290 --> 00:19:02.250
So you can see that in his work in the finance sector,

357
00:19:02.250 --> 00:19:04.620
Hanuman is guided by his values.

358
00:19:04.620 --> 00:19:06.840
He's not simply making money at any cost.

359
00:19:06.840 --> 00:19:08.970
He's thinking about the work he's doing

360
00:19:08.970 --> 00:19:11.130
and the impact that he can have

361
00:19:11.130 --> 00:19:12.540
and where he's working with companies

362
00:19:12.540 --> 00:19:14.340
that may not completely share his values.

363
00:19:14.340 --> 00:19:16.683
He wants to speak to them and persuade them.

364
00:19:19.470 --> 00:19:22.140
Hanuman summarizes his thoughts on dharma

365
00:19:22.140 --> 00:19:23.883
and emotional intelligence.

366
00:19:24.780 --> 00:19:26.793
We are all connected to each other.

367
00:19:27.930 --> 00:19:30.930
According to dharma, prosperity should be in the interests

368
00:19:30.930 --> 00:19:32.853
of the wealth of all beings.

369
00:19:34.110 --> 00:19:35.940
If we're driven by anger or greed,

370
00:19:35.940 --> 00:19:37.563
we'll generate selfishness.

371
00:19:38.730 --> 00:19:41.160
Meditation is a tool to balance the mind

372
00:19:41.160 --> 00:19:43.023
and make wise decisions.

373
00:19:43.980 --> 00:19:47.187
Having integrity and honesty will make you a better

374
00:19:47.187 --> 00:19:49.383
and more successful person.

375
00:19:50.970 --> 00:19:54.360
So Hanuman's argument is that being driven by values

376
00:19:54.360 --> 00:19:57.240
will actually make you a better, more successful person

377
00:19:57.240 --> 00:19:59.970
in the finance sector because you're considering

378
00:19:59.970 --> 00:20:02.493
and building trust and relationships.

379
00:20:04.050 --> 00:20:07.593
And these dharmic values can be lived by anyone.

380
00:20:10.890 --> 00:20:12.450
True or false?

381
00:20:12.450 --> 00:20:15.240
The dharmic value of ahimsa would encourage Hindus

382
00:20:15.240 --> 00:20:19.053
to invest finances in military or arms trade companies.

383
00:20:23.640 --> 00:20:24.750
It's false, isn't it?

384
00:20:24.750 --> 00:20:26.310
Because the dharmic value of ahimsa

385
00:20:26.310 --> 00:20:28.440
or non-violence would discourage Hindus

386
00:20:28.440 --> 00:20:31.953
to invest in finance in military or arms companies.

387
00:20:34.950 --> 00:20:37.800
Okay, let's draw all of our learning

388
00:20:37.800 --> 00:20:39.100
from this lesson together.

389
00:20:40.110 --> 00:20:40.943
I want you to imagine

390
00:20:40.943 --> 00:20:43.860
that you're working for a company in the finance sector

391
00:20:43.860 --> 00:20:46.203
and your manager has sent you this email.

392
00:20:47.257 --> 00:20:49.500
"Dear Laura, our client has asked

393
00:20:49.500 --> 00:20:51.300
to move the project deadline.

394
00:20:51.300 --> 00:20:52.650
The deadline currently falls

395
00:20:52.650 --> 00:20:55.020
during an important religious festival.

396
00:20:55.020 --> 00:20:56.400
They claim a large number

397
00:20:56.400 --> 00:20:58.140
of staff will be observing this festival

398
00:20:58.140 --> 00:20:59.730
and will be away from work.

399
00:20:59.730 --> 00:21:03.450
This makes it difficult for them to meet the original date.

400
00:21:03.450 --> 00:21:05.520
In my view, we should cancel the contract

401
00:21:05.520 --> 00:21:07.770
as they're clearly not up to the job.

402
00:21:07.770 --> 00:21:10.860
Please email them immediately to tell them this.

403
00:21:10.860 --> 00:21:12.780
I'm annoyed you didn't find this out before.

404
00:21:12.780 --> 00:21:15.030
It would've saved us a lot of money and effort.

405
00:21:15.030 --> 00:21:16.830
Don't let this happen again.

406
00:21:16.830 --> 00:21:17.663
Josh."

407
00:21:18.540 --> 00:21:21.243
So this is the email that your manager has sent you.

408
00:21:22.230 --> 00:21:25.620
I'd like you to read that again carefully

409
00:21:25.620 --> 00:21:27.690
and I'd like you to write a response to them,

410
00:21:27.690 --> 00:21:30.060
which shows good religious literacy

411
00:21:30.060 --> 00:21:32.850
and emotional intelligence.

412
00:21:32.850 --> 00:21:35.700
How would you reply in a way that didn't create negativity

413
00:21:35.700 --> 00:21:39.330
with your manager, but also try to preserve the relationship

414
00:21:39.330 --> 00:21:41.100
with your client?

415
00:21:41.100 --> 00:21:43.740
Think about this idea of trust.

416
00:21:43.740 --> 00:21:46.260
Think about the reasons why the client

417
00:21:46.260 --> 00:21:48.060
wants to move the deadline.

418
00:21:48.060 --> 00:21:50.280
How can you keep that client on board

419
00:21:50.280 --> 00:21:53.400
but also try and help your manager to understand

420
00:21:53.400 --> 00:21:57.030
in a positive way about the problems

421
00:21:57.030 --> 00:21:58.580
and how they could be overcome?

422
00:21:59.430 --> 00:22:02.340
You probably want to work and talk with someone about this.

423
00:22:02.340 --> 00:22:04.690
I look forward to seeing what you come up with.

424
00:22:10.290 --> 00:22:13.830
So this is my response. I wonder what yours was.

425
00:22:13.830 --> 00:22:16.500
I've said, "Dear Josh, I'm sorry to hear

426
00:22:16.500 --> 00:22:19.140
that the client has asked to move the project deadline

427
00:22:19.140 --> 00:22:22.047
and I apologize for any inconvenience it might cause."

428
00:22:22.920 --> 00:22:25.710
So straight away here, I've used my emotional intelligence

429
00:22:25.710 --> 00:22:27.720
to try and apologize

430
00:22:27.720 --> 00:22:30.180
and admit that I've got some responsibility.

431
00:22:30.180 --> 00:22:32.843
So I'm not gonna get angry with him

432
00:22:32.843 --> 00:22:35.707
and try to be too defensive.

433
00:22:35.707 --> 00:22:39.120
"However, I do not think we should cancel the contract.

434
00:22:39.120 --> 00:22:41.040
The festival only lasts a couple of days

435
00:22:41.040 --> 00:22:43.260
as an important part of the culture.

436
00:22:43.260 --> 00:22:44.490
If we can move the deadline,

437
00:22:44.490 --> 00:22:46.740
it will create good relationships with the client

438
00:22:46.740 --> 00:22:48.510
and I'm confident we'll be able to make up time

439
00:22:48.510 --> 00:22:49.740
on the project.

440
00:22:49.740 --> 00:22:51.090
If we can make this work,

441
00:22:51.090 --> 00:22:53.670
it may mean we attract new business in the future

442
00:22:53.670 --> 00:22:55.530
based on this relationship.

443
00:22:55.530 --> 00:22:57.237
Regards, Laura."

444
00:22:58.500 --> 00:23:00.810
So you can see what Laura's tried to do here.

445
00:23:00.810 --> 00:23:02.730
She's shown some religious literacy

446
00:23:02.730 --> 00:23:05.370
by explaining that the festival is only short,

447
00:23:05.370 --> 00:23:08.160
but it's a really important part of the culture.

448
00:23:08.160 --> 00:23:10.650
She said that if we could do what they stated,

449
00:23:10.650 --> 00:23:12.270
we'd create a good relationship

450
00:23:12.270 --> 00:23:14.760
and that might mean more work in the future.

451
00:23:14.760 --> 00:23:16.200
So Laura's trying to demonstrate

452
00:23:16.200 --> 00:23:18.270
why having good religious literacy

453
00:23:18.270 --> 00:23:20.940
and emotional intelligence could actually help the company

454
00:23:20.940 --> 00:23:22.530
financially in the future.

455
00:23:22.530 --> 00:23:24.390
So it's not just about being nice to people,

456
00:23:24.390 --> 00:23:27.510
it's also about helping and doing the right thing as well.

457
00:23:27.510 --> 00:23:29.220
And she's applying some of those values

458
00:23:29.220 --> 00:23:30.870
we talked about there, isn't she?

459
00:23:33.750 --> 00:23:36.030
Second question is this.

460
00:23:36.030 --> 00:23:38.190
I want you to imagine you're working for a company

461
00:23:38.190 --> 00:23:40.950
in the finance sector and a client has asked you

462
00:23:40.950 --> 00:23:44.400
for your advice about where to place their investments.

463
00:23:44.400 --> 00:23:47.340
In the first interview, they say they want to make profit

464
00:23:47.340 --> 00:23:49.940
but have not talked about what is important to them.

465
00:23:51.030 --> 00:23:53.490
Think about some of the ideas of dharma

466
00:23:53.490 --> 00:23:55.380
and the dharmic values that we learned about

467
00:23:55.380 --> 00:23:57.273
in our interview with Hanuman Dass.

468
00:23:58.260 --> 00:24:01.593
What values might you suggest they think about in investing?

469
00:24:02.550 --> 00:24:05.010
Should they just be purely motivated by profit

470
00:24:05.010 --> 00:24:06.360
or can you make any arguments

471
00:24:06.360 --> 00:24:09.060
for any other values they might need to think about?

472
00:24:09.060 --> 00:24:11.700
And where do you think you might suggest to invest in?

473
00:24:11.700 --> 00:24:15.243
And are there any areas you might suggest not investing in?

474
00:24:16.500 --> 00:24:18.750
You may want to draw on that interview

475
00:24:18.750 --> 00:24:20.553
from Hanuman Dass to help you.

476
00:24:26.400 --> 00:24:28.807
So you may have said something like that.

477
00:24:28.807 --> 00:24:32.040
"Investing should be something done wisely.

478
00:24:32.040 --> 00:24:34.470
It may not be best to think about quick profits,

479
00:24:34.470 --> 00:24:37.437
but having long-term values will be successful."

480
00:24:38.280 --> 00:24:40.200
You might advise that they work with companies

481
00:24:40.200 --> 00:24:42.420
that value people and the rest of the world.

482
00:24:42.420 --> 00:24:45.300
So perhaps not investing in companies that relate to arms

483
00:24:45.300 --> 00:24:46.830
or the animal industry.

484
00:24:46.830 --> 00:24:48.360
You might advise working with companies

485
00:24:48.360 --> 00:24:50.160
that are helping to make the transitions

486
00:24:50.160 --> 00:24:53.040
to help them slow climate change.

487
00:24:53.040 --> 00:24:54.930
And you might work with possible investors

488
00:24:54.930 --> 00:24:56.670
to speak to them about their plans

489
00:24:56.670 --> 00:25:00.150
and encourage them to work in an ethical way.

490
00:25:00.150 --> 00:25:01.983
So we're bringing some important values here

491
00:25:01.983 --> 00:25:05.280
that in finance, it may not just be about quick profits,

492
00:25:05.280 --> 00:25:08.070
but having relationships will make things successful

493
00:25:08.070 --> 00:25:09.840
in the long term.

494
00:25:09.840 --> 00:25:12.840
You might want to get from the client what values they have

495
00:25:12.840 --> 00:25:15.240
and then you can advise them accordingly.

496
00:25:15.240 --> 00:25:17.430
But also really important about the idea

497
00:25:17.430 --> 00:25:20.160
of working with companies over a long period of time

498
00:25:20.160 --> 00:25:22.710
and encouraging them to be more ethical

499
00:25:22.710 --> 00:25:26.193
rather than just being negative and shunting them away.

500
00:25:27.300 --> 00:25:29.223
I wonder what you came up with.

501
00:25:31.680 --> 00:25:34.440
So let's summarize our learning today.

502
00:25:34.440 --> 00:25:36.210
We've learned that the finance sector

503
00:25:36.210 --> 00:25:38.793
is an important employer in the British economy.

504
00:25:39.630 --> 00:25:42.150
We've learned that the finance sector is international

505
00:25:42.150 --> 00:25:44.343
and includes clients around the world.

506
00:25:45.210 --> 00:25:47.310
We've learned that having good religious literacy

507
00:25:47.310 --> 00:25:49.440
will mean better understanding of how people

508
00:25:49.440 --> 00:25:51.840
do business around the world and the cultures

509
00:25:51.840 --> 00:25:53.043
in different countries.

510
00:25:53.910 --> 00:25:55.740
We've learned that trust and relationships

511
00:25:55.740 --> 00:25:57.960
are critical to success in finance

512
00:25:57.960 --> 00:26:00.870
and that having good religious literacy

513
00:26:00.870 --> 00:26:02.400
and emotional intelligence

514
00:26:02.400 --> 00:26:05.073
will help you to make wise decisions.

515
00:26:06.060 --> 00:26:07.980
I really hope you've enjoyed this lesson today

516
00:26:07.980 --> 00:26:09.720
and enjoyed learning about the connections

517
00:26:09.720 --> 00:26:13.260
between having a good understanding of religions and beliefs

518
00:26:13.260 --> 00:26:16.710
and being successful in this industry.

519
00:26:16.710 --> 00:26:19.800
And I look forward to seeing you in another lesson soon.

520
00:26:19.800 --> 00:26:20.633
Thank you.

lessons.unitTitle: Religion or belief in the workplace: how do we work together?

lessonKeywords.description: a person who acts as a representative or promoter of a particular body or activity
treating all people fairly and equally
knowledge of how religions, worldviews and beliefs shape lives
a positive state determined by social, economic and environmental conditions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In the UK, the wellbeing sector is a growing industry and includes jobs that help improve physical and mental health.
Knowledge of religions and beliefs is extremely important to build relationships.
Knowing about different practices, such as dietary laws or periods of fasting, will improve client experiences.
Inclusivity is very important for people's wellbeing.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Religious views or fear of water, rooted in family history, may prevent some people feeling comfortable while swimming.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: People from racially minoritised communities choose not to participate in swimming.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how and why religious literacy is important for people working in wellbeing.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If appropriate and with sensitivity, the teacher could lead a discussion on the pupils' own experiences of access to swimming and water safety.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceLabel: Depiction or discussion of sensitive content
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Subjects which particular individuals may be sensitive to, eg, adoption, migration, bereavement or death, divorce, poverty, deprivation.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Ms. Ramalli, and thank you for joining me for today's RE lesson.

"Try to consume foods that are going to give you energy.

159
00:08:44.940 --> 00:08:49.290
This could be a bowl of oatmeal made with milk or water.

160
00:08:49.290 --> 00:08:50.790
You could add chia seeds,

161
00:08:50.790 --> 00:08:55.170
walnuts, and sliced bananas or even dates.

162
00:08:55.170 --> 00:08:58.623
These will release energy slowly throughout the day.

163
00:08:59.460 --> 00:09:03.780
Taking supplements will also help you maintain energy.

164
00:09:03.780 --> 00:09:06.330
There are companies that specialize

165
00:09:06.330 --> 00:09:08.730
in halal supplements.

166
00:09:08.730 --> 00:09:13.140
These are also suitable for vegans and vegetarians.

167
00:09:13.140 --> 00:09:16.920
Still come along to fitness classes but after iftar,

168
00:09:16.920 --> 00:09:19.137
once you have broken your fast."

169
00:09:21.840 --> 00:09:24.570
Katrina explains how as a Buddhist,

170
00:09:24.570 --> 00:09:27.873
she applies religious literacy in her own life.

171
00:09:29.347 --> 00:09:32.100
"As a Buddhist, I believe that exercise

172
00:09:32.100 --> 00:09:33.510
and staying healthy

173
00:09:33.510 --> 00:09:37.230
helps me feel present and practice mindfully.

174
00:09:37.230 --> 00:09:39.150
I'm also a vegetarian,

175
00:09:39.150 --> 00:09:41.160
so I fully understand

176
00:09:41.160 --> 00:09:44.577
why my clients have different needs and values."

177
00:09:48.000 --> 00:09:50.580
Select two ways that a personal trainer

178
00:09:50.580 --> 00:09:54.273
can show religious literacy to a client who is fasting.

179
00:09:55.200 --> 00:09:58.590
a, tell clients what they should eat or drink;

180
00:09:58.590 --> 00:10:01.620
b, offer advice on foods and drinks

181
00:10:01.620 --> 00:10:03.764
to avoid during fasting;

182
00:10:03.764 --> 00:10:07.560
or c, keep up to date on emerging products,

183
00:10:07.560 --> 00:10:09.843
for example, halal supplements.

184
00:10:17.160 --> 00:10:20.670
Well done if you said that b and c

185
00:10:20.670 --> 00:10:22.323
are the correct answers.

186
00:10:25.800 --> 00:10:29.160
So now we're going to complete a practice task.

187
00:10:29.160 --> 00:10:33.150
Andeep and Sofia were not sure how religious literacy

188
00:10:33.150 --> 00:10:37.350
was relevant to working in the wellbeing sector.

189
00:10:37.350 --> 00:10:39.870
Using the interview with Katrina,

190
00:10:39.870 --> 00:10:42.330
can you describe three ways

191
00:10:42.330 --> 00:10:45.390
in which she said having good religious literacy

192
00:10:45.390 --> 00:10:48.243
meant she was more effective in her job?

193
00:11:01.110 --> 00:11:02.400
So in your answers,

194
00:11:02.400 --> 00:11:05.673
you may have said the following points.

195
00:11:07.110 --> 00:11:08.640
In the wellbeing sector,

196
00:11:08.640 --> 00:11:11.610
religious literacy is really important.

197
00:11:11.610 --> 00:11:13.482
It helps her avoid stereotypes

198
00:11:13.482 --> 00:11:16.830
and assumptions about her clients.

199
00:11:16.830 --> 00:11:20.640
Not everyone practices their religion in the same way.

200
00:11:20.640 --> 00:11:21.960
Having these insights

201
00:11:21.960 --> 00:11:24.663
can help build better relationships.

202
00:11:26.310 --> 00:11:27.450
You may also have said

203
00:11:27.450 --> 00:11:30.960
that many religions follow dietary laws.

204
00:11:30.960 --> 00:11:33.240
Understanding religious dietary laws

205
00:11:33.240 --> 00:11:37.290
is essential for Katrina to offer inclusive, safe,

206
00:11:37.290 --> 00:11:39.960
and effective nutritional guidance.

207
00:11:39.960 --> 00:11:43.233
For example, halal supplements to Muslim clients.

208
00:11:44.520 --> 00:11:47.490
And thirdly, good religious literacy

209
00:11:47.490 --> 00:11:49.530
will mean adapting nutrition

210
00:11:49.530 --> 00:11:52.920
and exercise programs around clients

211
00:11:52.920 --> 00:11:55.800
who fast for longer periods of time.

212
00:11:55.800 --> 00:11:59.310
She needs to advise on which foods are best to avoid

213
00:11:59.310 --> 00:12:01.620
and which foods should be included

214
00:12:01.620 --> 00:12:03.843
in order to maintain energy.

215
00:12:07.410 --> 00:12:10.290
So that leads us to the second part of today's lesson

216
00:12:10.290 --> 00:12:13.080
on religion and worldview in wellbeing.

217
00:12:13.080 --> 00:12:14.190
And in this part of the lesson,

218
00:12:14.190 --> 00:12:15.360
we are going to be exploring

219
00:12:15.360 --> 00:12:18.033
religious literacy and inclusivity.

220
00:12:19.736 --> 00:12:23.583
Andeep and Sofia are discussing their learning so far.

221
00:12:24.823 --> 00:12:28.440
Andeep says, "I can see how religious literacy

222
00:12:28.440 --> 00:12:30.900
could be useful in wellbeing now.

223
00:12:30.900 --> 00:12:32.040
But is it just enough

224
00:12:32.040 --> 00:12:34.947
to know about different religions and beliefs?"

225
00:12:36.030 --> 00:12:38.790
Sofia says, "Well, we know how Katrina

226
00:12:38.790 --> 00:12:42.360
uses religious literacy to meet the needs of clients.

227
00:12:42.360 --> 00:12:44.787
I wonder if there may be other ways?"

228
00:12:46.260 --> 00:12:47.400
What do you think?

229
00:12:47.400 --> 00:12:49.413
Can you think of any examples?

230
00:12:56.953 --> 00:12:59.303
Andeep and Sofia meet Melona Headley

231
00:12:59.303 --> 00:13:01.851
at the careers fair.

232
00:13:01.851 --> 00:13:05.670
Melona Headley is the founder of Bold Waters,

233
00:13:05.670 --> 00:13:07.800
a social impact movement

234
00:13:07.800 --> 00:13:11.703
using nature and open water to increase wellbeing.

235
00:13:14.537 --> 00:13:18.513
Melona explains the vision behind Bold Waters.

236
00:13:19.920 --> 00:13:22.530
Melona says, "I founded Bold Waters

237
00:13:22.530 --> 00:13:23.970
because each year,

238
00:13:23.970 --> 00:13:28.053
hundreds of lives are lost to drowning in the UK.

239
00:13:28.950 --> 00:13:32.190
Many of these deaths are preventable.

240
00:13:32.190 --> 00:13:33.979
They happen in open water

241
00:13:33.979 --> 00:13:37.770
and disproportionately affect young people

242
00:13:37.770 --> 00:13:41.493
from racially minoritized and low-income communities.

243
00:13:42.510 --> 00:13:47.510
In 2023, 236 people died

244
00:13:47.550 --> 00:13:50.523
from water-related incidents in the UK.

245
00:13:51.390 --> 00:13:53.580
The vision of Bold Waters

246
00:13:53.580 --> 00:13:57.690
is to remove barriers by increasing swim access,

247
00:13:57.690 --> 00:13:59.580
water safety education,

248
00:13:59.580 --> 00:14:02.337
and connection with natural spaces."

249
00:14:04.230 --> 00:14:07.593
How does Bold Waters aim to remove barriers?

250
00:14:14.580 --> 00:14:17.190
Well, Bold Waters aims to remove barriers

251
00:14:17.190 --> 00:14:21.420
by increasing swim access, water safety education,

252
00:14:21.420 --> 00:14:23.853
and connection with natural spaces.

253
00:14:26.010 --> 00:14:30.570
Bold Waters aims to increase inclusivity and wellbeing

254
00:14:30.570 --> 00:14:33.030
by getting more young people

255
00:14:33.030 --> 00:14:34.650
from racially minoritized

256
00:14:34.650 --> 00:14:38.670
and low-income communities outdoors and in nature,

257
00:14:38.670 --> 00:14:40.170
encouraging young people

258
00:14:40.170 --> 00:14:44.070
to participate safely in outdoor swimming,

259
00:14:44.070 --> 00:14:47.793
and teaching young people how to be safe around water.

260
00:14:50.700 --> 00:14:53.940
Amina is an ambassador for Bold Waters.

261
00:14:53.940 --> 00:14:56.940
Amina has a Muslim worldview.

262
00:14:56.940 --> 00:14:59.610
Amina says, "I'm currently studying

263
00:14:59.610 --> 00:15:01.645
public services at college.

264
00:15:01.645 --> 00:15:03.510
I want to help people.

265
00:15:03.510 --> 00:15:05.790
When I heard about Bold Waters

266
00:15:05.790 --> 00:15:09.810
and their work to increase inclusivity and water safety,

267
00:15:09.810 --> 00:15:11.403
it spoke to my heart.

268
00:15:13.020 --> 00:15:16.500
My family are from a small village in Bengal.

269
00:15:16.500 --> 00:15:18.900
My mum grew up scared of the water,

270
00:15:18.900 --> 00:15:20.520
and so was I.

271
00:15:20.520 --> 00:15:24.600
Having swim lessons wasn't part of my childhood.

272
00:15:24.600 --> 00:15:28.530
I'm Muslim and have grown up in a culture of modesty.

273
00:15:28.530 --> 00:15:30.870
Religious fuse may prevent people

274
00:15:30.870 --> 00:15:33.267
from feeling comfortable while swimming."

275
00:15:37.650 --> 00:15:40.110
Amina explains why religious literacy

276
00:15:40.110 --> 00:15:42.397
is important to her.

277
00:15:42.397 --> 00:15:44.130
"As a youth ambassador,

278
00:15:44.130 --> 00:15:46.890
I have seen how people's ethnicity

279
00:15:46.890 --> 00:15:49.500
and where they grow up affects their experience

280
00:15:49.500 --> 00:15:52.200
of swimming and water safety.

281
00:15:52.200 --> 00:15:55.230
As a Muslim, I was able to share religious literacy

282
00:15:55.230 --> 00:15:57.330
through my insights.

283
00:15:57.330 --> 00:16:01.980
I know the importance of having inclusive open spaces

284
00:16:01.980 --> 00:16:05.280
where Muslim girls feel comfortable to swim.

285
00:16:05.280 --> 00:16:07.110
Swim spaces where Muslim girls

286
00:16:07.110 --> 00:16:09.630
do not need to wear their hijab.

287
00:16:09.630 --> 00:16:12.450
Having inclusivity is really important

288
00:16:12.450 --> 00:16:14.097
for people's wellbeing."

289
00:16:16.920 --> 00:16:18.420
True or false?

290
00:16:18.420 --> 00:16:20.340
Religious literacy promotes

291
00:16:20.340 --> 00:16:22.593
inclusivity and wellbeing.

292
00:16:27.660 --> 00:16:30.900
Well done if you said that statement is true.

293
00:16:30.900 --> 00:16:32.700
Religious literacy most definitely

294
00:16:32.700 --> 00:16:35.013
promotes inclusivity and wellbeing.

295
00:16:36.878 --> 00:16:38.403
Andeep and Sofia ask Melona,

296
00:16:39.427 --> 00:16:43.347
"How does Bold Waters promote inclusivity and wellbeing?"

297
00:16:44.490 --> 00:16:48.930
Melona replies, "At Bold Waters, all are welcome.

298
00:16:48.930 --> 00:16:52.950
It is important that our participants feel safe, seen

299
00:16:52.950 --> 00:16:57.390
and included in order to improve water safety.

300
00:16:57.390 --> 00:17:01.260
Our sessions aim to reduce fear around water.

301
00:17:01.260 --> 00:17:04.290
Our instructors are trained to be respectful

302
00:17:04.290 --> 00:17:06.930
and know that a child's fear of water

303
00:17:06.930 --> 00:17:09.750
might be rooted in family history,

304
00:17:09.750 --> 00:17:12.870
not just the present moment.

305
00:17:12.870 --> 00:17:15.600
This approach ensures inclusivity

306
00:17:15.600 --> 00:17:17.727
and increases wellbeing."

307
00:17:19.410 --> 00:17:22.203
How does Bold Waters promote wellbeing?

308
00:17:30.396 --> 00:17:32.167
Andeep and Sofia ask,

309
00:17:32.167 --> 00:17:34.650
"As a youth ambassador for Bold Waters,

310
00:17:34.650 --> 00:17:37.107
how do you promote inclusivity?"

311
00:17:38.850 --> 00:17:42.420
Amina says, "As an ambassador for Bold Waters,

312
00:17:42.420 --> 00:17:46.560
I'm representing other girls and women like me.

313
00:17:46.560 --> 00:17:48.090
Children are malleable

314
00:17:48.090 --> 00:17:52.470
and it is important to have representation and inclusivity

315
00:17:52.470 --> 00:17:54.963
so they can see people who look like them.

316
00:17:55.830 --> 00:17:58.140
Offering female-only swimming lessons

317
00:17:58.140 --> 00:18:00.510
with female instructors and lifeguards

318
00:18:00.510 --> 00:18:03.537
is another way to promote inclusivity."

319
00:18:06.480 --> 00:18:10.710
A Bold Waters session can include participants

320
00:18:10.710 --> 00:18:14.790
being in cold water, such as a lake or river,

321
00:18:14.790 --> 00:18:18.720
learning lifesaving skills whilst fully clothed,

322
00:18:18.720 --> 00:18:21.543
and learning how to float without panicking.

323
00:18:23.550 --> 00:18:26.580
Amina explains about one of the Bold Waters programs

324
00:18:26.580 --> 00:18:28.023
that she's involved in.

325
00:18:28.897 --> 00:18:31.560
"I'm involved in Global Flow.

326
00:18:31.560 --> 00:18:33.660
This is a six-month leadership

327
00:18:33.660 --> 00:18:35.359
and employability program,

328
00:18:35.359 --> 00:18:39.420
including swim qualifications, mentorship,

329
00:18:39.420 --> 00:18:43.320
and a four-week international teaching placement.

330
00:18:43.320 --> 00:18:46.890
This involves traveling to countries such as Thailand,

331
00:18:46.890 --> 00:18:48.570
where there are high drowning rates

332
00:18:48.570 --> 00:18:50.790
amongst young children.

333
00:18:50.790 --> 00:18:52.860
The Global Flow instructors

334
00:18:52.860 --> 00:18:55.050
teach locals how to swim,

335
00:18:55.050 --> 00:18:57.690
and they then teach others.

336
00:18:57.690 --> 00:19:01.200
My hope is that a small ripple makes a big wave

337
00:19:01.200 --> 00:19:03.777
and generations will learn to swim."

338
00:19:06.540 --> 00:19:08.610
Select two ways an organization

339
00:19:08.610 --> 00:19:10.985
can promote inclusivity.

340
00:19:10.985 --> 00:19:14.760
a, ensure a representative workforce;

341
00:19:14.760 --> 00:19:18.150
b, train employees on religious literacy;

342
00:19:18.150 --> 00:19:22.443
and c, make assumptions about religions and worldviews.

343
00:19:28.440 --> 00:19:31.740
Well done if you selected a and b.

344
00:19:31.740 --> 00:19:35.010
Two ways an organization can promote inclusivity

345
00:19:35.010 --> 00:19:37.614
is by ensuring a representative workforce

346
00:19:37.614 --> 00:19:40.653
and training employees on religious literacy.

347
00:19:43.511 --> 00:19:46.320
So now you are going to create a press release

348
00:19:46.320 --> 00:19:49.530
showcasing the work of Bold Waters.

349
00:19:49.530 --> 00:19:50.700
In your press release,

350
00:19:50.700 --> 00:19:53.760
include the following information.

351
00:19:53.760 --> 00:19:57.780
What is Bold Waters and why was it founded?

352
00:19:57.780 --> 00:20:01.620
How does it aim to remove barriers to water safety?

353
00:20:01.620 --> 00:20:04.770
And how does Bold Waters promote religious literacy?

354
00:20:04.770 --> 00:20:06.903
And why is that important?

355
00:20:18.600 --> 00:20:20.040
Okay, welcome back.

356
00:20:20.040 --> 00:20:23.160
Your responses may look something like this.

357
00:20:23.160 --> 00:20:24.030
So you may have said,

358
00:20:24.030 --> 00:20:27.000
Bold Waters is a social impact movement

359
00:20:27.000 --> 00:20:30.873
using nature and open water to increase wellbeing.

360
00:20:31.800 --> 00:20:35.070
It was founded in response to hundreds of lives

361
00:20:35.070 --> 00:20:36.930
being lost in the UK

362
00:20:36.930 --> 00:20:40.410
each year due to drowning in open waters.

363
00:20:40.410 --> 00:20:43.002
Many of these deaths disproportionately

364
00:20:43.002 --> 00:20:46.710
affect young people from racially minoritized

365
00:20:46.710 --> 00:20:48.693
and low-income communities.

366
00:20:51.390 --> 00:20:55.290
Bold Waters aims to remove barriers to water safety

367
00:20:55.290 --> 00:20:59.010
by increasing swim access, water safety education,

368
00:20:59.010 --> 00:21:01.473
and connection with natural spaces.

369
00:21:02.850 --> 00:21:05.884
One way that Bold Waters promotes religious literacy

370
00:21:05.884 --> 00:21:08.700
is through inclusivity.

371
00:21:08.700 --> 00:21:09.990
As a youth ambassador,

372
00:21:09.990 --> 00:21:14.220
Amina offers representation for Muslim females.

373
00:21:14.220 --> 00:21:16.830
Amina can give personal insights

374
00:21:16.830 --> 00:21:20.100
into the barriers that Muslims females can face

375
00:21:20.100 --> 00:21:22.623
when learning to swim and be water safe.

376
00:21:23.730 --> 00:21:24.990
But this is important

377
00:21:24.990 --> 00:21:27.690
because it ensures the important message

378
00:21:27.690 --> 00:21:31.413
on water safety is given to the right communities.

379
00:21:33.900 --> 00:21:36.210
So that brings us to the end of today's lesson

380
00:21:36.210 --> 00:21:38.523
on religion and worldview in wellbeing.

381
00:21:39.540 --> 00:21:41.373
Here is a summary of our learning.

382
00:21:42.300 --> 00:21:44.310
The wellbeing sector includes any job

383
00:21:44.310 --> 00:21:47.460
that helps improve physical health, mental health,

384
00:21:47.460 --> 00:21:49.983
emotional balance, or quality of life.

385
00:21:50.880 --> 00:21:53.760
Religious literacy helps build positive relationships

386
00:21:53.760 --> 00:21:56.013
with clients in the wellbeing sector.

387
00:21:57.300 --> 00:21:58.740
People working in wellbeing

388
00:21:58.740 --> 00:22:01.620
may need to know about different religious practices,

389
00:22:01.620 --> 00:22:04.473
dietary requirements, and respecting modesty.

390
00:22:05.430 --> 00:22:09.150
Bold Waters aims to remove water safety barriers

391
00:22:09.150 --> 00:22:13.200
for racially minoritized and low-income communities.

392
00:22:13.200 --> 00:22:16.350
One way that Bold Waters promotes religious literacy

393
00:22:16.350 --> 00:22:18.090
is by having an inclusive

394
00:22:18.090 --> 00:22:20.880
and representative advisory board.

395
00:22:20.880 --> 00:22:23.856
Ambassadors can more effectively identify

396
00:22:23.856 --> 00:22:27.783
and reach the right audiences with important messages.

397
00:22:28.920 --> 00:22:30.300
Thank you very much for joining me

398
00:22:30.300 --> 00:22:32.100
for your RE lesson today,

399
00:22:32.100 --> 00:22:34.053
and I hope to see you again soon.

lessons.lessonTitle: Religion and worldviews in your employment
lessons.unitTitle: Religion or belief in the workplace: how do we work together?

lessonKeywords.description: the ability to recognise, understand, manage, and effectively respond to your own emotions and the emotions of others
knowledge of how religions, worldviews and beliefs shape lives
the fundamental beliefs and core principles that define what is most important to you

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Religious literacy is valuable in careers where interacting respectfully with diverse communities is essential.
Being knowledgeable about beliefs and practices can foster trust and strengthen professional relationships.
Religious literacy can enhance emotional intelligence by encouraging empathy, awareness and sensitivity toward others.
Core values like honesty and compassion create positive working relationships across all fields of employment.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Religious literacy develops skills and values that are valuable across many professions including healthcare, wellbeing, finance and hospitality.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Studying religion and worldviews only prepares you to become a clergy member or work in a church or other religious institution.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how and why religious literacy and emotional intelligence will be connected to my future career.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could teach this lesson alongside careers education or option choices.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello there.
My name is Mr. Robertson, and I'm delighted to welcome you to this RE lesson today.
Today's lesson is the final lesson in our unit, which has been asking the question, "Religion and Belief in the Workplace: How do we work together?" This lesson is entitled "Religion and Worldviews in Your Employment." And in this lesson, you're going to be reflecting on the sort of career that you might want in the future and how religion, worldviews, understanding of different beliefs will intersect and help you in that career.
So the outcome for today's lesson is this.
I can explain how and why religious literacy and emotional intelligence will be connected to my future career.
We have some key words that will help guide us today and help us understand our lesson more deeply.
Our first words are religious literacy.
And by that, we mean a knowledge of how religions, worldviews, and beliefs shape lives.
Our second words are emotional intelligence, and that is the ability to recognize, understand, manage, and effectively respond to your own emotions and the emotions of others.
And finally, we have the word values.
And by values, we mean the fundamental beliefs and core principles that define what is most important to you.
Today's lesson is in two parts.
In the first part of the lesson, we're gonna be thinking about religious literacy and its importance.
So let's just recap what exactly we mean by this term, religious literacy.
So having a religious literacy or being religiously literate means being able to understand and engage thoughtfully with religion and belief as it's lived and expressed in society.
It includes understanding that religions and beliefs are diverse and they change over time.

lessons.lessonTitle: Gautama Buddha's life and its significance

lessonKeywords.description: a life free from worldly pleasures, and involves giving up material possessions
an awakened or enlightened person
a state of wisdom that enables total clarity and understanding of the truths of existence
Siddhartha Gautama’s experience of illness, old age, death and a holy man
reaching enlightenment

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are divergent beliefs about whether the life story of Gautama Buddha is factual or illustrative.
Before birth, there were signs that Siddhartha Gautama would be significant.
He gave up his life of luxury with his wife after seeing the Four Sights.
The Four Sights included sickness, old age, death and an ascetic.
He eventually reached enlightenment, became known as the Buddha and established the Sangha.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some Buddhists interpret all the stories as factual, while others see them as illustrative. Most Buddhists believe that the stories contain spiritual truths.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All Buddhists believe that the stories of the life of the Buddha are factual.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson content could to be taught over more than one lesson.

lessonKeywords.description: literally 'Greater Vehicle'
reaching enlightenment
the nature of all beings, which means that all beings can become enlightened/reach Buddhahood
literally ‘emptiness’

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Mahayana Buddhism, the skandhas that make up a human are seen as empty.
Sunyata helps Buddhists to understand that there is no fixed, stable self, and the universe is neither fixed nor stable.
This is because everything is dependent on something else and nothing has its own form.
Buddha-nature is important in Mahayana Buddhism and means all humans have the potential to become enlightened.
Teachings on the human personality influence Buddhists to avoid attachments, meditate daily and show compassion.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sunyata refers to the emptiness of inherent existence, meaning that all things are empty of an independent, permanent or fixed essence.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sunyata means that everything is completely nonexistent, there is nothing at all, or the world is a void with no meaning or value.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the Mahayana Buddhist belief in the human personality, why it is important and how it influences Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The story of Nagasena and the Chariot helps explain the concept of sunyata.

Hello, I'm Ms. Ramalli, and thank you for joining me for today's RE lesson.
Today's lesson forms part of our unit on Buddhism and beliefs, and we're going to be exploring the human personality in the Mahayana tradition.
Today's lesson outcome is I can explain the Mahayana Buddhist belief in the human personality, why it is important, and how it influences Buddhist today.
To help guide us through today's lesson, there are four key words.
Mahayana, sunyata, Buddhahood, Buddha-nature.
Mahayana, literally means Greater Vehicle, sunyata literally translates as emptiness, Buddhahood is reaching enlightenment, and Buddha-nature refers to the nature of all beings, which means that all beings can become enlightened and reach Buddhahood.
So today's lesson on the human personality in Mahayana tradition takes two parts.
So we're going to begin by learning about the Mahayana beliefs on the human personality, and then we move on to consider the importance and influence of these beliefs.
Mahayana means Greater Vehicle, and this school of Buddhism focuses on achieving enlightenment for the sake of all beings.
Mahayana Buddhism is practised by the majority of people in China, Tibet, Japan, South Korea, and Vietnam.
Mahayana Buddhism includes Tibetan, Pure Land, and Zen Buddhism.
Many Mahayana Buddhists aim to become enlightened, but they delay nibbana to help teach enlightenment to others.
Many Mahayana Buddhists believe in the concepts of sunyata, Buddha-nature, and attaining Buddhahood.
Okay, let's complete a check for understanding.
Which of the following concepts are important in Mahayana traditions? A, attaining Buddhahood, B, sunyata, C, nibbana, can be referred to as nirvana, and D, Buddha-nature.
We're looking for three concepts for this answer.
Pause a video here and press play when you're ready to check your answers.
Well done if you selected A, B, and D as the correct answers.
The term sunyata has its origins in the ancient Sanskrit language.
So sunya, meaning empty or void, and the ta is a quality or state of being, which is equivalent to the English term ness.
So sunyata can be interpreted to mean emptiness.
Sunyata can be understood as meaning that everything depends on something else.
This links to the Buddhist belief in dependent arising or paticcasamuppada.
The five aggregates or skandhas that make up a human are seen as empty, and sunyata can be understood as being very similar to anatta, the belief in no self, which is one of the three marks of existence.
Okay, let's complete a check for understanding.
What is the meaning of sunyata? A, reaching enlightenment, B, a being destined for enlightenment who postpones their final escape from samsara in order to help living beings, or C, emptiness.
Well done if you selected C as the correct answer.
Tashi is a Mahayana Buddhist, and she explains the meaning of sunyata.
Tashi says, "Imagine a soap bubble.
At first, it seems real and solid, but when it pops, it disappears, leaving nothing behind.
Sunyata is like realising that everything in life is a bit like that bubble.
It might seem solid, but it's not as permanent as it appears." Ting, a Mahayana Buddhist monk explains his belief in sunyata.
Ting says, "I believe everything in life is constantly changing.
Nothing is permanent.
Sunyata is about understanding that nothing stays the same forever.
Sunyata may be seen as a rewording of anatta.
There is no fixed or unchanging self or soul inside us.
We are made up of thoughts, feelings, and experiences that are always changing, and there's no unchanging me at the core." Mike is a British Mahayana Buddhist and works as a scientist.
He further explains the meaning of sunyata.
Sunyata is a belief that everything in the world is interconnected.
Just as we are made up of countless tiny cells and atoms, the world around us is interconnected in a web of causes and effects.
Sunyata encourages us to see the connections between all things.
Now let's use the analogy of a chair to consider and understand the nature of Sonata.
So here we have on our screen an example of a chair.
Now, the idea of the chair is that there is no fixed self or essentially essence that forms the chair because the chair is made up of many different parts.
All of those parts are interrelated and interconnected.
So essentially it relies on all parts to actually function as a chair.
This chair is not permanent, so at some point, the chair can get damaged and broken, and it will no longer be used and considered as a chair.
Essentially, the chair is empty of independent existence.
Okay, let's complete a check for understanding.
Which one of the following does not explain sunyata? A, emptiness, B, everything is permanent, C, there is no fixed self, or D, everything is interconnected.
Well done if you selected B as the correct answer, the idea of Buddha-nature or tathagatagarbha is particularly important in Mahayana Buddhism.
It translates from the Sanskrit word tathagatagarbha.
Tathata, one who has come garter, gata, the one who has gone, and garbha, womb or embryo.
The Buddha achieved enlightenment and became the one who has gone, but he stayed to help others, so he's also the one who has come.
Therefore to tathagata refers to the Buddha.
Buddha-nature is the concept that every individual carries the essence or nature of a Buddha within themselves.
This means that all beings can become enlightened and reach Buddhahood.
An individual's Buddha-nature can be obscured by ignorance, cravings, and attachments to the material world.
When a person fully grasp the Buddha's Dhamma teachings, they achieve Buddhahood, and this will reveal the Buddha-nature that has always been present.
Okay, let's complete a check for understanding.
What is the meaning of Buddha-nature? A, reaching enlightenment, B, a being destined for enlightenment who postpones their final escape from samsara in order to help living beings, or C, the nature of all beings, which means that all beings can reach Buddhahood.
Well done if you said the correct answer that the meaning of Buddha-nature is C.
So it's the nature of all beings, which means that all beings can reach Buddhahood.
In Buddhist scripture, the analogy of bees and honey is used to describe Buddha-nature, tathagatagarbha.
Buddha-nature is like honey that is encircled by a swarm of bees.
The honey is sweet and desirable, but cannot be accessed due to the bees.
The only way to taste the honey is to remove the bees.
Similarly, a person must eliminate distraction such as cravings, desire, and attachments to attain Buddhahood.
The Parable of the Burning House from the Lotus Sutra.
One day, a fire broke out in the home of a wealthy man who had many children.
The man shouted to his children inside the burning house, urging them to flee.
However, the children were so engrossed in their games that they didn't pay attention to his warning even as the flames spread.
In response, the wealthy man came up with a clever plan to get the children to leave the house.
Knowing they loved interesting toys, he called out, "Listen, outside the gate are the carts you've always dreamed of, carts pulled by goats, carts pulled by deer, and carts pulled by oxen.
Come out and play with them.
He knew these would be irresistible to them.
The children excited by the idea of these new toys eagerly ran outside, but instead of the carts he had mentioned, the father presented them with a cart far more magnificent than any they had imagined.
One draped in precious stones and drawn by white bullocks.
The key was that the children were saved from the dangers of the burning house.
In this parable, the father symbolises the Buddha, and the sentient being, which are living beings with consciousness, represent the children trapped in the burning house.
The burning house stands for the world consumed by the fires of ageing, sickness, and death.
The Buddhist teachings are akin to the father's attempt to guide the children away from temporary pleasures towards a far greater joy, nibbana.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Pure Land Buddhism follows the teaching of Amitabha (Amida) Buddha.
Amitabha (Amida) Buddha features in Mahayana texts.
He was a king who achieved enlightenment and created a kingdom free from suffering (a pure land).
A goal of Pure Land Buddhists is to be reborn here.
Alongside other Buddhist teachings, Pure Land Buddhists follow Amitabha (Amida) as a role model.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Some Pure Land Buddhists may believe this, while others believe it is a place to be reborn. The Pure Land is a land free from suffering and distractions, making it a more accessible place to attain enlightenment and achieve Buddhahood.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Pure Land is nibbana (nirvana).

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the history and nature of the Pure Land and how it influences Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Research the history of Pure Land Buddhism in Japan by exploring the teachings of Honen (1133-1212) and the developments made by his disciple Shinran (1173-1263).

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: One of the most important teachings of the Buddha are the Four Noble Truths, which explain suffering and its end.
The analogy of a doctor is a common way to understand these teachings and involves observation, cause and cure.
Ignorance, greed and hatred - known as the three poisons - are explained as the cause of suffering.
The Four Noble Truths influence Buddhists to act in different ways, including avoiding attachments and cravings.
The Eighfold Path contains guiding principles which will help Buddhists achieve this.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Buddhists would argue that the teachings are realistic. Knowing and understanding the reality of suffering releases them from that suffering.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Buddha's teachings on suffering are negative and pessimistic.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of the Four Noble Truths and how they influence Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Print out a copy of the three poisons for pupils to annotate.

lessonKeywords.description: the teachings of the Buddha
a belief that all life includes suffering and unsatisfactoriness
safety or shelter from difficulty or danger

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Dhamma has a variety of meanings depending on its context.
It is a central Buddhist belief and Buddhists may believe that it upholds natural order.
Dhamma is based upon the actions and teachings of the Buddha, which Buddhists are encouraged to follow.
These teachings were later written down and are now also known as the Dhamma.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In Buddhism, Dhamma refers to the teachings of the Buddha.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Dhamma or Dharma has the same meaning for all dharmic worldviews.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the different meanings of Dhamma and how it influences Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use an audio recitation of the Three Refuges for slide 12.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Theravada Buddhism, a human is understood to be a combination of five elements known as the Five Aggregates(Skandhas)
A human is made up of Five Aggregates (Skandhas) – body, sensation, perception, thoughts and consciousness.
This helps Buddhists to understand the concept of 'no-self'.
Understanding the truth about existence and the self helps Buddhists understand ultimate reality.
Theravada Buddhists are influenced by the Five Aggregates (Skandhas) to avoid attachments and cravings.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Five Aggregates are constantly changing, and none of them are permanent or fixed. Each aggregate is subject to impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). They show that there is no independent, permanent self.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Five Aggregates represent a "self" or a "soul" that are permanent or fixed.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the Theravada Buddhist belief in the human personality and how this influences Theravada Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Create a case study of a famous individual. Ask pupils to identify how the person has changed physically, emotionally and mentally over the years. Link this case study to the Five Aggregates (Skandhas) to highlight the Buddha's teaching on non-self (anatta).

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Sermon at Benares was a teaching point used by the Buddha to help people understand suffering.
The nature of life, including old age, sickness and death contributes to suffering.
Change and impermanence are also significant contributors to the suffering we experience.
Many Buddhists believe suffering is essential to help us understand ultimate reality and choose how to live.
The Buddha's teachings on the causes of suffering influence Buddhists e.g. to stop cravings.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Buddhism views suffering (dukkha) as an essential part of life. It’s not about denying suffering but understanding its nature and learning to live in a way that reduces unnecessary suffering.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Buddhism teaches that suffering is inherently bad or to be avoided at all costs.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain different states of suffering, the causes of suffering and how these influence Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could include further teachings on the three marks of existence, the Four Noble Truths and the three poisons to consolidate learning in this lesson.

the cycle of birth, life, death and rebirth

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The end of suffering and ability to reach Nibbana is the Fourth Noble Truth.
The Four Noble Truths help Buddhists understand what is meant by 'The Middle Way'.
The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta contains teaching on key Buddhist beliefs including Nibbana.
Most Buddhists believe Nibbana is the end of suffering and can be attained by all people.
Reaching Nibbana may depend on how fully you enact the Eightfold Path.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Nibbana is the cessation of suffering, craving and ignorance. It is the end of the cycle of rebirth and the realisation of true peace and freedom.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Nibbana (Nirvana) is a Buddhist view of heaven.

lessonKeywords.description: a spiritual experience that opens a person up to the highest state of consciousness
a method of meditation; a state of calmness
a method of meditation focused on insight into the true nature of things
a method of meditation focused on developing  pure love which is selfless and not possessive

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Meditation is a significant Buddhist practice.
It can be a means to making progress in the stages of the Eighfold Path.
There are many different types of meditation, but samatha and vipassana are the main types.
Buddhists may also do metta bhavana meditation, which focuses on loving kindness.
Meditation influences most Buddhists to develop mindfulness and deepen their wisdom of the Buddha's Dhamma.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Meditation can involve observing and acknowledging thoughts without getting attached to them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Meditation requires clearing the mind completely of all thoughts.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the nature, purpose and significance of meditation in Buddhism and how it influences Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Complete a research project on samatha and vipassana meditation. Compare and contrast the similarities and differences.

lessonKeywords.description: causes of dukkha that affect all beings: ignorance, greed and hatred
the inability to see things as they really are
the attachment to material things and the ongoing selfish desire for more
a feeling of intense dislike, anger; wishing others harm

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The three poisons are represented on the Wheel of Life as greed (cockerel), ignorance (pig) and hatred (snake).
Buddhist teachings say the three poisons are the root of suffering (dukkha).
There are diverse interpretations between Buddhists of the Wheel of Life and the three poisons.
Belief in the three poisons influences Buddhists thoughts, beliefs and actions in different ways.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: How Buddhists interpret and respond to the three poisons depends on the school of Buddhism they follow.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That all Buddhists interpret and respond to the three poisons in the same way.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the three poisons, why they cause suffering and how they influence Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson can be linked to the second Noble Truth (Samudaya) on the causes of suffering.

lessons.lessonTitle: Human destiny: the Arhat and Boddhisatva ideals

lessonKeywords.description: a state of wisdom that enables total clarity and understanding of the truths of existence
a perfected person; in Theravada Buddhism, this is a term for a person who has become enlightened
in Mahayana Buddhism, this is an enlightened being who remains in the cycle of samsara in order to help others achieve enlightenment
the path a Buddhist will take to achieve enlightenment

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mahayana means ‘great vehicle’, which refers to the idea of the Bodhisattva path as a ‘vehicle’ to Buddhahood.
The Theravada Arhat path is sometimes called the 'lesser vehicle', but this is less common due to negative connotations.
When a person follows the Arhat path, they seek perfection in understanding and enacting the Buddha's teachings.
An Arhat sees pleasure as a distraction and aims to completely remove craving and desires.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: An Arhat might be viewed as a fully enlightened being focused on their own liberation, while a Bodhisattva is someone who seeks to bring others along on the path to enlightenment.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Arhats (Arahants) and Bodhisattvas are essentially the same and share identical goals.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain Buddhist beliefs on human destiny and how these beliefs influence Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Link with teachings on the six paramitas (perfections).

lessonKeywords.description: the three divisions of the Eightfold Path: ethics, meditation, and wisdom
the belief that individuals can achieve a state of perfect peace where they experience liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth
insight into the true nature of reality
moral principles that inform behaviour and attitudes
a spiritual experience that opens a person up to the highest state of consciousness

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: This is another name for the Eightfold Path, split into categories.
It contains the three aspects: ethics, meditation and wisdom.
Right action, speech and livelihood are a part of 'ethics'.
Right mindfulness, effort and concentration come under 'meditation'.
Right view and intention are categorised as 'wisdom'.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Each element strengthens the others. They are not isolated practices but interconnected stages on the path to attaining nibbana (nirvana), liberation from the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Threefold Way categories can be practiced independently or in isolation.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the Threefold Way, why it is important and how it influences Buddhists.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson links with learning on the Eightfold Path.

lessonKeywords.description: the belief that everything exists because other things do; everything is interconnected and everyone affects everyone else
the belief in cause and effect, intentions and actions will affect the future
twelve links of causation
the cycle of birth, life, death and rebirth
a symbolic representation of the cycle of samsara

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Dependent arising is a fundamental concept across schools of Buddhism.
Everything arises and exists in dependence on multiple causes and conditions.
There is a 12 link chain of causation.
The twelve links include matters of thought, feeling and change.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Dependent arising emphasises the interdependent nature of all things.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That dependent arising means everything exists in a deterministic way and that all things are fixed and dependent on conditions.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the concept of dependent arising and how it influences Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Print a copy (in colour if possible) of the Tibetan wheel of life for each student to analyse.

lessonKeywords.description: a belief that nothing is permanent
a belief that there is no fixed self/no soul
a belief that all life includes suffering and unsatisfactoriness

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: These are three fundamental marks (or signs) of reality, sometimes also called the Three Universal Truths.
Anicca reminds Buddhists that nothing is fixed or stable.
Buddhism teaches that a person's feelings, beliefs and character, even their soul, changes.
The story of Nagasena and the Chariot is used to explain the idea of having ‘no self’.
The impermanence of existence (anicca) means that pleasant experiences do not last.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The three marks of existence are meant to help Buddhists understand life so they can live more freely and peacefully by accepting change, letting go of attachments and thereby reducing suffering.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The three marks of existence, in particular dukkha, only describe negative aspects of life.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the three marks of existence and how they influence Buddhists today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Sensistive content: this lesson makes reference to the lack of a permanent self (anatta) and suffering (dukkha), which could raise questions or discussions around death.

They are anicca, anatta, and dukkha.

Anatta is a belief that there is no fixed self, or no soul.
And dukkha is a belief that all life includes suffering and unsatisfactoriness.

The Buddha taught that there are three characteristics that are universal to all things.
These are known as the three marks of existence, or some people refer to them as the Three Universal Truths.
They are dukkha, all life involves suffering, anicca, nothing is permanent, and anatta, there is no fixed self, or no soul.
Dukkha is a key Buddhist concept meaning suffering or unsatisfactoriness.
There are different types of dukkha.
There's suffering, such as physical and mental pain.
So, for example, breaking an arm would be causing physical pain and some mental pain as well.
Dukkha is also caused by attachment.
So, for example, having strong bonds, or affection, or desires to people or objects.

Anicca means nothing is permanent and is the second mark of existence.
The Buddha taught that anicca applies to all things.
It applies to living things because birth is followed by growth, then decay, and death.
It also applies to non-living things.
So, for example, like a Buddhist temple will eventually erode if it's not repaired.
And anicca also applies to a person's thoughts, feelings, and emotions, all of which change and evolve over time.
The concepts of dukkha and anicca can be understood through a popular story in Buddhist tradition, the story of Kisa Gotami.
Kisa Gotami, a young woman from Savatthi, India, was devastated when her son suddenly died.
In her grief, she refused to accept his death, believing that with the right medicine, he could be revived.
She carried his lifeless body through the streets, asking everyone she met for a cure.
However, no one could offer her a solution and gently tried to help her accept the reality of her loss.
But she was determined to find a way to save him.
Eventually, Kisa Gotami was directed to the Buddha, who promised to give her medicine to revive her son.
He told her to find a mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died.
Eagerly, Kisa Gotami began her search, confident that she would find the seed.
But everywhere she went, she learned that death had touched every household.
This realisation slowly made her understand that death was a part of life and that she was not alone in her suffering.
As Kisa Gotami continued her search, she began to grasp the universality of death.
She saw that every family had lost someone, whether it was a child, a partner, or a parent.
With this understanding, her perspective shifted.
She no longer saw her loss as unique but as part of the natural cycle of life.
Eventually, she returned to the Buddha, accepting her son's death.
Kisa Gotami was suffering because of the attachment to her son and ignorance about the impermanent nature of all things.
The Buddha explained that the true medicine he had offered was not for her son but for her understanding.
Through her journey, she had learned a crucial lesson about impermanence, anicca, and the inevitability of death.
The Buddha taught her that suffering, dukkha, is a natural part of life and that understanding this truth is an essential part of the Buddha's dharma.
After this experience, Kisa Gotami became a follower of the Buddha.

"Nagasena and the Chariot." The Buddhist story of "Nagasena and the Chariot" is used to explain the concept of anatta, or no-self.
The story takes place in the "Milinda Panha," a Buddhist text in which King Milinda engages in a series of dialogues with the monk Nagasena.
One day, King Milinda, curious about the nature of the self, asked Nagasena, "Who are you?" Nagasena replied, "I am Nagasena." King Milinda then asked, "What is the nature of Nagasena? The body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness are merely parts of a person, but they do not constitute a permanent, unchanging self.
To help illustrate his point, Nagasena asked the king, "Your majesty, when you speak of a chariot, what do you mean? Do you refer to the wheels, the axle, the frame, the horses, or the reigns?" King Milinda replied, "I refer to all of them together as the chariot." Nagasena then asked, "But is there anything in the chariot that is a chariot in and of itself? Is it the wheels, the axle, the frame, the horses, the reigns?" The king thought for a moment and answered, "No, none of those parts individually are the chariot." Nagasena explained, "Just as the term chariot is used to describe a collection of parts, but no single part is the chariot itself, the term Nagasena is used to describe the collection of the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness.

lessonKeywords.description: also known as ‘The Middle Way', it includes the way to wisdom and mental training
an important part of the Buddha’s teachings, explaining the truth about existence
a state of wisdom that enables total clarity and understanding of the truths of existence
a source of wisdom and authority that includes some of the most famous teachings of the Buddha, including the Eightfold Path

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The final Noble Truth is the path to enlightenment, called the Eightfold Path.
The Eightfold Path is also known as the Middle Way by many Buddhists.
Each part of the path can help a Buddhist end suffering.
The eight stages are guiding principles which lead to enlightenment when simultaneously perfected.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Eightfold Path is more like a guide that can be practiced simultaneously and in an integrated way. Buddhists don’t have to master one step before moving to another; instead, they work on all aspects together.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Eightfold Path is a set of steps to be followed in a strict, linear order.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the Eightfold Path, why it is important and how it influences Buddhists.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The learning in this lesson links to the lessons on the Four Noble Truths and the Threefold Way.

lessonKeywords.description: the justice of Allah, from Al-Adl (The Just)
Allah as all loving, generous and kind; one of Allah’s 99 Names
Allah is present and active in the world.
Allah is all powerful.
Allah is above, beyond, and independent of the world.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: In Islam Allah is believed to be omnipotent, beneficent, merciful, fair and just. Surah 46:33 supports this.
In Islam Allah is believed to be both transcendent and immanent.
There are different perspectives within Islam on these different attributes of God.
The justice of God, Adalat, is a key belief in Shia Islam.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Al Adl (the just) is one of the 99 names of Allah and is important to Sunni Muslims as well as Shia but it isn't in the six articles of faith and may be seen as part of a believe in Tawhid - the oneness of God.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That Sunni Muslims do not believe in the justice of Allah (Adalat) because it is not mentioned in the six articles of faith.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what Muslims believe about the nature of Allah and some different Muslim perspectives on this.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can read lists of the other 99 names of Allah in order to learn more about Muslim beliefs about the nature of Allah.

lessonKeywords.description: a pilgrimage in Islam where many of the steps of Ibrahim are followed
the worship of idols, forbidden in Islam
son of Ibrahim who rebuilt the Ka'aba with him
important prophet in Islam, also known as Abraham
a sacred cube-shaped building in Makkah

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: All of the prophets in Islam had a message of the oneness of Allah.
Ibrahim had a revelation of monotheism in his polythesitic society.
Muslims celebrate the obedience of Ibrahim with Id ul-Adha.
The steps of Hajj and the Ka'aba are linked to the life of the Prophet Ibrahim.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In the Qur'an, Ibrahim is questioning the way other people are worshipping the sun, moon and stars - he does not worship them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Ibrahim worshipped the sun, moon and stars before discovering Allah's oneness.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the role and importance of the Prophet Ibrahim in Islam.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can research and link the Muslim practices of Salah and Hajj to the story of and importance of the Prophet Ibrahim.

lessonKeywords.description: bringing a child into existence through reproduction
belief in and worship of only one God, Allah
worshipping anything other than Allah, considered to be the worst sin in Islam
belief in Allah’s oneness and unity

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Islam is monotheistic, and the God referred to is the God of Abrahamic religions.
There are several references in the Qur'an, including 3:18 and Surah 112.
Shirk is the contradiction of Tawhid and is a serious sin in Islam.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Allah is Arabic for 'The God' and the Qur'an teaches that Allah is the God of the Abrahamic faiths. Moses/Abraham/Jesus and others are all significant prophets in Islam, and known through Arabic spellings of their names; they are the same prophets.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That Muslims believe Allah is a different 'god' to the God of Christianity and Judaism.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what a belief in Tawhid is, and why this is important for Muslims.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can apply each of the practices of the Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts and show how they are supported by a belief in Tawhid.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Prophethood is a key belief for all Muslims.

lessons.lessonTitle: Authority of other sacred texts in Islam

lessonKeywords.description: altered from its original divine form
Injeel, revelation given to Prophet Jesus (Isa)
the holy books in Islam
Zabur, revelation given to Prophet David (Dawud)
Tawrat, revelation given to Prophet Moses (Musa)

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Belief in the holy books of Islam is a key belief for Muslims.
The Torah, Gospel, Psalms and Scrolls (of Ibrahim) are all sacred texts in Islam.
The Qur'an teaches Muslims that these texts have been corrupted over time.
The Qur'an corrects understandings from those texts for Muslims.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Torah, Gospel, Psalms and Scrolls of Abraham also have authority for Muslims but according to Muslim teachings, their message has become corrupted over time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That the Qu'ran is the only holy book that has authority for Muslims.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of holy books in Islam, other than the Qur'an.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can link to the understandings of the Torah and Gospels in Christianity and compare and contrast key aspects of this.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The imamate is one of the five roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam.
The imamate refers to specific leaders as guides of Islam following the death of the Prophet Muhammad.
Shi'a Muslims believe Ali was chosen to be the Prophet Muhammad's successor and first Imam.
All of the Imams following Ali were born of the Prophet's bloodline, and were infallible.
The belief in imamate helps shape Shi'a beliefs and practices.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Prophet Muhammad was the final prophet and the Imams are not believed to be prophets or divine beings in any way. They were without sin and rightly chosen to lead the community after the death of the final Prophet Muhammad.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That Shi'a Muslims belive the Imams are Prophets or divine beings in some way.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of the imamate within Shi'a Islam.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Students can link aspects of the life stories of the Imams especially Imam Ali and Imam Hussein to important Shi'a Muslim practices especially Ashura and Id ul-Ghadeer.
