lessons.lessonTitle: Ian McCormack and near death experience
lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: a complete transformation, often involving a change in worldview, such as adopting a new religious belief
a man who converted to Christianity after having a near death experience
a transformative experience often involving visions, feelings of peace or encounters with a higher power, typically reported by those who have been close to death
a philosopher who argues that religious experiences should be taken as evidence for the existence of God

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: People may have religious experiences that confirm their current beliefs or convert them to a new religious outlook.
Ian McCormack was an atheist who had a near death experience and became a Christian.
Following his near death experience and conversion, he has dedicated his life to spreading Christianity.
Richard Swinburne argues the role of credulity and testimony support the validity of religious experiences.
Philosophers may argue that whether his experience can be proven is less significant than the impact it has had.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: McCormack’s experience is similar to those in other religions, where people report encounters with divine beings or light, showing such experiences aren’t unique to Christianity.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Ian McCormack’s experience is unique and proves the truth of Christianity.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can reflect on Ian McCormack’s conversion experience and use philosophical arguments to show how it could be used as support for the existence of God.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers could show a clip of Ian McCormack sharing his testimony or parts of the film about his experience 'The Perfect Wave'. Task B could be adapted as an oracy task or cloze task using the sample answers (students are presented text with key elements missing for them to complete).

496
00:27:33.240 --> 00:27:35.430
that Ian McCormack's near death experience

497
00:27:35.430 --> 00:27:38.373
led to his conversion to Christianity,

498
00:27:39.750 --> 00:27:41.670
Ian McCormack's near death experience

500

lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: understanding or information believed to be true and supported by reasons
a French town where St Bernadette’s visions of Mary occurred, now a pilgrimage site
a girl who reported visions of Mary in 1858, inspiring the Lourdes pilgrimage
the mother of Jesus, particularly honoured in Catholicism as pure and a helper in prayer
a religious experience where a person sees or feels a divine or spiritual presence

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Bernadette experienced visions of the Virgin Mary, who asked for a chapel to be built by a nearby muddy cave.
Mary told her to drink the muddy water of the spring and the next day it flowed with clear water.
Her body is said by the Catholic Church to remain internally incorrupt and she was named a saint.
Lourdes is a place of pilgrimage for Christians, with the water said to have healing properties.
Some philosophers would argue that Bernadette gained knowledge of God although others would disagree.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many, including her family and Church authorities, questioned her mental state, and her visions were only accepted by the Church as genuine following investigation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: St Bernadette's visions were believed by everyone at the time.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what St Bernadette learned through her visions and reflect on whether she had knowledge of God.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task B could be completed as an extended writing task with students writing paragraphs using their learning on St Bernadette to answer the question 'Do religious experiences prove God exists?'. It could also form the basis of an oracy task with students role-playing or debating the question.

lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: the spark of Brahman or spirit within all living beings
the supreme spirit or ultimate reality
philosopher who argues for religious pluralism
conflicting religious experiences challenge the idea they can prove the existence of God
someone who believes that different religions are paths to understanding the same divine truth

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Atman is a Sanskrit word for the true or eternal self and most Hindus believe it is in every living being.
Atman comes from Brahman and could be seen as a part of the ultimate being within each of us.
In different Indian philosophies, atman is part of the individual self and ultimate reality or completely separate.
The multiple claims issue is the problem that conflicting religious experiences challenge the proof of one specific God.
John Hick argues that religious pluralism means different religious experiences interpret the same divine reality.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: While atman is similar to the soul, in Hinduism, it's not only the individual self but also connected to the larger, ultimate reality (Brahman). So, it’s more than just an individual soul; it can be seen as part of everything.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Atman is just like the soul in other religions.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain different understandings of the atman as divine and evaluate the claim that experiences across religions cancel each other out.

teacherTips.teacherTip: An introduction to atman, Brahman and reincarnation in Hindu Dharma might be a useful preliminary task.

lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: facts or information that supports an idea
a device that stimulates the temporal lobes with electromagnetic fields to induce religious experiences
a neuroscientist known for developing the God helmet to study the brain's role in religious experiences
a philosophical tool that encourages questioning and doubting things to ensure we have good evidence before believing them

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The God helmet is an experiment designed to see if feelings of religious experience can be induced.
In the experiment, the temporal lobe is stimulated based on testimony of those with temporal lobe epilepsy.
The stimulation brought about effects similar to those of people claiming a religious experience.
Some claim this experiment proves God does not exist, or at least that religious experience is not genuine.
Others argue that a creator God designed the human brain to include the temporal lobe as a channel of communication.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In reality, the experiment has not been consistently replicated, and the results have been debated.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The God helmet experiment has been reliably replicated and proves that religious experiences are just caused by brain stimulation.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain Persinger’s God helmet experiment and evaluate its implications for the existence of God.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For additional material A, encourage discussion about how points in the story could be understood differently. Task B part 2 could be used as an extended writing activity or a cloze task (using the sample answer with gaps for students). Teachers could search online for a picture of the God helmet.

lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: a religious experience where someone feels a deep personal connection to a higher power
a philosophical approach that assesses ideas based on their usefulness in real-life situations
personal feeling or moment when someone believes they connect with a higher power
20th century psychologist and philosopher who popularised pragmatism

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: William James studied religious experiences from a psychologist's perspective and explained their impact on philosophy.
He relied on observation, conversation and evidence of impact to reach his conclusions.
William James identified four features of mystical experience.
He did not seek to prove the existence of a particular God or gods.
William James concluded that his research leads to a likelihood of a god existing.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: James' investigtions led him to be agnostic and open to the idea of God rather than to be a believer.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Students may think James had a clear view on the existence of God.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain William James' understanding of religious and mystical experiences and how they contribute to the question of God's existence.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Task C could be used as either an oracy or an extended writing task.

lessons.unitTitle: Knowing God: does religious experience prove God exists?

lessonKeywords.description: Arabic word for God (literally means 'the God')
used by Sufis to describe deep, personal knowledge of Allah that comes from spiritual experiences
a way of experiencing and connecting with Allah through personal, inner experiences
a mystical approach in Islam that focuses on achieving ma’rifah (true knowledge of Allah) through a deep, personal connection with him

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sufism may be described as Islamic mysticism
Sufis exist within Sunni and Shi'a Islam, rather than being a distinct religious group.
Sufi Muslims try to achieve direct personal experience of Allah.
Other Muslims may disagree with the idea of trying to get personal experience of God.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sufis can be either Sunni or Shi'a, athough the majority are Sunni.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sufism is a branch of Islam, like Sunni and Shi'ism.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Sufis connect with Allah and why some Muslims would say knowledge cannot be gained through Sufi mysticism.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You might like to show a video of whirling. Task B2 could become an oracy task or cloze task (providing the answer with key gaps to fill).

lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: all people having the same rights and opportunities
the act of eating together in rows, signifying equality and unity
the community of Sikhs who meet and worship in the gurdwara
a process of collecting, analysing and interpreting data

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: At the time Sikh Gurus lived, women experienced fewer opportunities than men.
The experiences of Guru Nanak's sister, Bibi, helped shape his views on the treatment of women.
The Guru Granth Sahib states that men and women are equal because God made them.
Sikh women are encouraged to study, participate and lead worship equally with men.
Data shows there may still be inequalities between men and women in lived experience.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sikh women have always played an active and important role, historically, as activists and modern day professionals.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sikh women are not as involved as men in religious and community life.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use the tools of social science to explain Sikh teachings on women and the role of Sikh women historically and today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use the British Sikh Reports (available online) to research other important issues to Sikhs living in Britain.

lessons.lessonTitle: Society at the time of Guru Nanak
lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: a social hierarchy, dividing people in society
the unfair treatment of a people and groups based on a part of their identity such as sex, race or religion
all people having the same rights and opportunities
the living Guru and main source of authority for Sikhs; a collection of writings from the ten Gurus and other important writers

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Society at the time of Guru Nanak impacted his beliefs and actions.
Key influences were the behaviour of Mughal rulers, the treatment of women and the caste system.
The teachings of Guru Nanak influence the lives of Sikhs today.
Sikhs can also turn to the Guru Granth Sahib to find Sikh teachings on equality.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The caste system was applied to people of different religions.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The caste system only applied to Hindus.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain what Indian society was like at the time of Guru Nanak and the impact of this on his views on equality.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Show students a timeline which also has this time period on it, and look at what else was happening in the world at the same time, e.g., Henry VIII's reign.

lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: an official count or survey, especially of a population
a group of people who leave their home country and live in different parts of the world
a Sikh place of worship, where people gather to pray, learn, and share meals together
a person's character or personality

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: There are Sikhs living all around the world, the largest population is in India, followed by Canada and Britain.
Data shows many British Sikhs identify as 'British Sikh' showing how important this identity is.
There are Sikhs represented in Britain in the House of Parliament.
Sikhs may proudly demonstrate both their national and religious heritage. For example, by supporting the Khanda poppy.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Sikh diaspora includes many people from countries in East Africa e.g. Uganda.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The Sikh diaspora are all immigrants from the Punjab region, now in India and Pakistan.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the meaning of Sikh diaspora and the importance of identity for Sikhs living in Britain today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask students to consider the challenges that the Sikh diaspora may have faced when first moving to Britain.

lessons.lessonTitle: The importance of the kirpan to Sikhs
lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: a group of people committed to living according to Sikh teachings
a short sword or knife with a curved blade, worn as one of the five signs of the Sikh Khalsa
temporal power, relationship with the world
spiritual power, relationship with Waheguru
God

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The kirpan is one of the 5 Ks and is worn by Khalsa Sikhs.
It does not have a direct translation into English, but the cloest is 'dagger, knife or sword'.
This can lead to a misunderstanding that the kirpan serves a violent purpose.
It is used in celebrations, at festivals and is also a symbol of core Sikh beliefs, such as equality and justice.
There are two kirpans in the Sikh symbol, called 'Miri' and 'Piri'; each has their own smbolic meaning.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The kirpan is a ceremonial and religious article carried by initiated Khalsa Sikhs as a symbol of their duty to stand up against injustice, not to harm others. It is one of the 5 Ks that represent Sikh identity and commitment to Waheguru (God).
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The kirpan is a weapon carried for violent purposes.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the symbolism of the kirpan and why it is important to Sikhs today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To consolidate learning in the lesson, you could watch a video clip which outlines the importance of the 5 Ks to Khalsa Sikhs.

lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: ‘princess’ - the name given to female members of the khalsa
the group of Sikhs that have a commitment to following Sikhi, including wearing the Panj Kakkars (5 Ks)
‘lion’ - the name given to male members of the khalsa

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Your name may impact how people perceive you and could reveal things about your heritage.
Indian last names might reveal the 'caste' or 'varna' to which your family belong and signifies social hierarchy.
Guru Gobind Rai established the Khalsa and Khalsa Sikhs may take 'Singh' or 'Kaur' after their name.
The names 'Singh' and 'Kaur' come from the Sanskrit for 'lion' and 'princess'.
By removing ties to the caste system, these new names may help to remove social hierarchy and show equality among Sikhs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: 'Singh' and 'Kaur' have also become used as a surname.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can only have the names 'Singh' or 'Kaur' if you are a Khalsa Sikh.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain why the names Singh and Kaur are important in Sikhi and how Princess Sophia Duleep Kaur Singh promoted equality.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teach the story of Guru Gobind Rai (Singh) and the Panj Payre to consolidate the learning in this lesson.

lessons.unitTitle: Social justice: how might Sikhs promote equality?

lessonKeywords.description: refers to material or financial service
the community or ‘free kitchen’ in a gurdwara
refers to mental or emotional service
helping others selflessly, an important Sikh value
refers to physical service

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Sikhs have many beliefs, but there are three known as 'golden rules'.
They are to remember God constantly, earn an honest livelihood, and to share with others.
Selfless Sewa contributes to these principles by ensuring people are never too self important to serve others.
Sewa may be tan (physical), man (mental), or dhan (material), meaning all Sikhs are able to perform Sewa in some way.
Examples can include serving at the Gurdwara (tan), offering counselling and advice (man) or through donations (dhan).

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Sikhi emphasises that sewa can be of three types: physical service, mental or emotional service or material and financial service.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Sewa in Sikhi is limited to physical labour, especially tasks like cleaning the Gurdwara, cooking in the langar (community kitchen), or serving food.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of sewa for Sikhs in Britain today.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Share examples of sewa (selfless service) within your nearest Sikh community.

lessons.lessonTitle: Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement
lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: one of Kenya’s largest ethnic groups or micro-nations
a person who campaigns to bring about political or social change
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people
the idea that God gave humans control over nature
the idea that humanity should look after the world God has created

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Wangari Maathai was a Kenyan environmental activist who became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Wangari Maathai started the Green Belt Movement to plant trees in Kenya and fight for women's rights.
Wangari Maathai’s worldview blended her indigenous Kikuyu beliefs with Catholic Christianity.
She argued that the land was sacred and was exploited by colonialism and ideas of dominion from the Bible.
She emphasised re-reading the Bible alongside indigenous beliefs to argue against the exploitation of land.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Wangari Maathai blended her Catholic and Kikuyu beliefs to argue for environmental justice in Kenya. She framed this through a distinctively African theological lens.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Environmental activism and protest is primarily a European concern.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Wangari Maathai's worldview inspired her environmental activism.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Wangari Maathai was an inspirational speaker. You may wish to find clips of her speaking. Her story 'The Little Hummingbird' is very simple, and in it she discusses how no-one is too small to make a change.

lessons.lessonTitle: Delores S. Williams and womanist theology
lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: the ability to endure hardship and keep moving forward
persevering through systemic oppression, despite the challenges of racism, sexism and discrimination
highlights Black women’s struggles, strength and faith, addressing both race and gender

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Williams overcame segregation, personal loss, and societal challenges to become a pioneering womanist theologian.
Her book 'Sisters in the Wilderness' shifted the focus of Christian faith to survival, community, and justice.
Her womanist theology empowers Black women, highlighting their resilience and faith.
Williams' womanist retelling of Hagar's story is significant to many African American women.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Many Black women find strength in their faith and ability to survive hardship, not because God removes their suffering, but because His liberating presence sustains them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Liberation is not always about escaping suffering.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Delores S. Williams’ worldview influenced her development of womanist theology.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Focus on Hagar’s perspective by exploring her resilience and faith through her emotional journey. Encourage students to view her not as a victim, but as a woman of strength and agency, shaped by her experiences and her relationship with God.

lessons.lessonTitle: Mercy Amba Oduyoye and African Women's theology
lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: focuses on empowering women by integrating their experiences into theological discussions
an indigenous belief system and culture primarily in Ghana and Ivory Coast
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people
a system of society where men hold most power and make key decisions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Oduyoye showed that African identity and Christianity can be blended rather than being in conflict.
She created a space for African women to shape theology and challenge male-dominated religious traditions.
She encouraged and reimagined areas of theology, such as Christology, from an African woman's perspective.
Her influence continues to inspire African women to lead, rethink and engage in theology.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: African women have unique experiences and should share their own stories. Others can support them, but real representation comes from their own voices, not others speaking for them.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: African women’s experiences and theology can be adequately represented by either white women or African men.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how Mercy Oduyoye’s worldview influenced her development of African Women’s theology.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For further reading, look at Dr Oluwatomisin Oredein.

lessons.lessonTitle: Coptic Christianity: Desert Fathers and Mothers
lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: belonging to part of the Christian church which began in Egypt
a religious practice of withdrawing from the world to pursue spiritual devotion
a religious man living in spiritual discipline and seclusion
someone who lives simply, giving up comforts to focus on growing spiritually
someone who chooses to live away from other people often in a remote place

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The Coptic church in Egypt is one of the most ancient Christian churches. Tradition says it was started by St Mark.
The Desert Fathers and Mothers were people who chose to live a life as hermits and ascetics in the desert.
The life of St Antony was hugely influential on important figures in western Christianity such as St Augustine.
Figures such as Desert Fathers and Mothers help us understand the diversity of Christian worldviews better.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The Coptic church shows that Christianity had spread to the continent of Africa many centuries before the impact of colonialism.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Christianity spread from the Middle East to Europe and that is where the most ancient forms of Christianity began.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the features of the Coptic church and the impact of Desert Fathers and Mothers.

teacherTips.teacherTip: There is a rich and distinctive tradition of Coptic art. You might want to find different examples to show students as well as exploring the restoration of the monastrey of St Anthony in Egypt.

lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: a family member from the past who has died, believed to offer guidance and protection
a practice for understanding spiritual guidance and finding one's Orisha
a branch or denomination within Candomblé
a divine ancestor or spirit; intermediaries between humans and the supreme god, Oludumaré

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion, shaped by Indigenous beliefs and Catholic influence.
It developed as spiritual survival during enslavement, blending Orisha worship with Catholic practices.
Despite oppression and legal bans, Candomblé endured through oral tradition, music, and ritual.
Through divination, priestesses seek messages from the Orishas to guide people through life’s challenges and decisions.
The faith honours connection - to nature, ancestors, and the divine.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Candomblé is an ancient African faith shaped by enslavement. While some include Catholic elements for tradition or protection, many focus purely on African roots. It’s a living, evolving religion adapting to each generation’s needs.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Candomblé always embraces Catholic elements.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the history of Candomblé and understand some of the ways it is practised.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Several videos and images of drumming and the Yemanjá festival are available online to enhance this section of the lesson.

lessons.unitTitle: Christianity: how have the experiences of the Global South shaped it?

lessonKeywords.description: existing naturally or having always lived in a place
someone who lives simply, giving up comforts to focus on growing spiritually
blessed; women who lived religious lives without formal vows or entering a convent
the process of declaring a deceased person a saint
taking control of a country and exploiting the resources and people

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Saint Rose of Lima was born in Peru to a Spanish father and an indigenous mother.
She was known for her beauty, but rejected marriage and led a life of prayer and solitude.
She was canonised as the first saint in the American continent and is known as the patron saint of indigenous peoples.
Colonisation of South America devastated the indigenous population. Saint Rose is hugely popular with Peruvians today.
Her following can be seen in requests at her sacred well and in her influence on a theology directed to the poor.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Saint Rose of Lima was the first saint to be canonised from the South American continent. She was Peruvian and is seen as a patron saint of indigenous peoples.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All saints canonised by the Roman Catholic Church are European.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the importance of Saint Rose of Lima and her influence today.
